title: The Sedna Hunter's Wife
summary: A Cree hunter's wife is taken by the wind and must navigate the spirit world to return home, aided by the animals she once cared for.
full_text:
There was once a Cree hunter named Wâsakâm who lived with his wife, Kisêwâtisiw, on the banks of a great river in the northern forest. They were poor but happy. Wâsakâm hunted caribou and moose, and Kisêwâtisiw tended the fire and smoked the meat. They had no children, but they loved each other deeply.

One winter, the cold was so fierce that even the wolves stayed in their dens. The river froze solid, and the snow piled so high that the trees bent under its weight. Wâsakâm went out to hunt, and Kisêwâtisiw stayed home to tend the fire.

She was alone for three days. On the third night, she heard a sound at the door — not a knock, but a whisper, like breath on glass. She opened the door, and the Wind walked in.

It was not a gust. It was a presence — tall, formless, cold beyond cold. It moved through the cabin like smoke, and where it passed, the fire died. The water in the kettle froze. The fur on the walls turned to ice.

Kisêwâtisiw tried to scream, but the Wind filled her mouth. She tried to run, but the Wind filled her lungs. She felt herself being lifted — not thrown, but drawn, like a leaf in a current. The cabin walls dissolved. The roof vanished. She was outside, naked, in the snow, and the Wind was carrying her north.

She flew over the forest. The trees were white and still, like skeletons. The sky was green with aurora, and the stars were sharp as knives. The Wind carried her past the treeline, past the tundra, to the place where the ice meets the sky.

There, at the edge of the world, she found a camp. It was not a human camp — it was a spirit camp, where the animals gathered when the world was young. She saw caribou walking on two legs, wearing human clothes. She saw bears sitting around a fire, speaking in Cree. She saw wolves playing a drum game, their paws striking the skin in perfect rhythm.

An old woman sat at the center of the camp. She had white hair and eyes like river ice. She wore a coat of ptarmigan feathers, and her hands were the hands of a caribou — hooves that held a pipe.

'You are Kisêwâtisiw,' the old woman said. 'I am Atê (the grandmother). The Wind brought you because you were kind to the animals. You thanked the caribou for its meat. You spoke to the river when you fetched water. You left offerings at the edge of the forest. We have watched you.'

Kisêwâtisiw wept. 'I want to go home,' she said. 'My husband will return from hunting, and I will not be there.'

Atê nodded. 'You may go home. But first, you must do something for us. The spirit world is out of balance. The animals forget their names. The seasons forget their order. The rivers forget their paths. You must help us remember.'

Kisêwâtisiw did not know how to help spirits remember. But Atê showed her. She gave her a drum — small, made of caribou skin — and told her to sing. 'Sing the songs your mother taught you,' Atê said. 'Sing the songs of the earth. Sing until the spirits remember who they are.'

Kisêwâtisiw sang. She sang the caribou song, and the caribou remembered their migration paths. She sang the bear song, and the bears remembered their caves. She sang the river song, and the river remembered its course. She sang all night, and by dawn, the spirit world was in balance again.

Atê smiled. 'You have done well. Now go home.'

The Wind carried Kisêwâtisiw back. She landed at her door, warm and whole. The fire was burning. The cabin was warm. Wâsakâm was home, frantic with worry.

'Where were you?' he cried.

Kisêwâtisiw told him everything. Wâsakâm did not believe her. But that spring, when the caribou migration came, every hunter in the village noticed something strange: the caribou were fat and healthy, fatter than any had been in years. And they walked right past Kisêwâtisiw's cabin, as if paying respects.

From that day on, Kisêwâtisiw was known as a keeper of the old ways. She sang the spirit songs every evening, and the animals thrived. When she died, many years later, the caribou migration paused at her grave, and the wind carried her song north, to the spirit camp at the edge of the world.
moral: Kindness to animals is kindness to the spirits. Those who honor the natural world are honored in return.
source: Based on Cree oral traditions from northern Canada.

title: The Marten's Wife
summary: A Cree hunter marries a woman who is secretly a marten spirit, and when she returns to the forest, he must choose between his world and hers.
full_text:
There was once a Cree hunter named Okimaw who lived at the edge of the boreal forest. He was a good hunter — fast, quiet, and patient. He could track a caribou for three days without tiring. But he was lonely. His wife had died the previous winter, and his lodge was cold.

One morning, walking through the forest, he found a woman sitting by a stream. She was beautiful — her hair was the color of autumn leaves, her skin was the color of birch bark, and her eyes were bright and quick. She wore a coat of marten fur, soft and brown.

'Who are you?' Okimaw asked.

'I am Mistikôs,' she said. 'I have no home. I have no family. I am alone.'

Okimaw brought her to his lodge. They married. Mistikôs was a good wife — she cooked, she sewed, she sang softly in the evenings. But there were strange things about her. She never ate meat. She flinched at the sound of traps. And at night, when she thought Okimaw was sleeping, she slipped out of the lodge and ran through the forest on all fours.

Okimaw pretended not to notice. But one night, he followed her. He crept through the trees, silent as a shadow, and watched her run. She ran fast — faster than any human — leaping over logs, sliding under branches, her body low to the ground. She ran to the river and dove in. She swam like an otter, her body twisting through the water.

Then she stopped. She stood in the middle of the river, the water at her waist, and she began to change. Her legs shortened. Her arms became shorter. Her skin turned to fur — brown, soft, glossy. Her face narrowed into a snout. Her tail grew long and bushy.

She was a marten.

Okimaw watched from the bank. His wife — his beautiful Mistikôs — was a marten spirit. She had taken human form to be with him. But she could not stay human forever. She needed the forest. She needed to run. She needed to be what she was.

Okimaw returned to the lodge. He sat by the fire and waited. When Mistikôs returned, shivering and wet, he did not speak. He did not ask questions. He held her close and warmed her by the fire.

In the morning, she was gone.

Okimaw searched for her. He walked the forest for days, calling her name. He followed marten tracks through the snow. He found marten dens in hollow trees. But Mistikôs did not appear.

On the fourth day, he found her sitting by the same stream where they had met. She was in human form again, but she was crying.

'I cannot stay,' she said. 'The forest calls me. The cold calls me. I am a marten, Okimaw. I was a marten before I was your wife, and I will be a marten after.'

Okimaw sat beside her. 'Then go,' he said. 'But come back sometimes. Come back in winter, when the lodge is cold. Come back in spring, when the salmon run. Come back whenever you want.'

Mistikôs looked at him. 'You would let me go?' 

'I love you,' Okimaw said. 'But I will not trap what was never mine to keep.'

Mistikôs smiled — a quick, bright smile, like a marten's face when it finds a bird's nest. She kissed his hand. Then she dropped to all fours, and the fur came, and she was a marten again. She leaped into the forest and was gone.

But she came back. Every winter, when the snow was deep, Okimaw would find a marten sitting on his doorstep. He would open the door, and the marten would enter. It would curl up by the fire, and Okimaw would talk to it — telling it about the hunt, the weather, the village news. And in the morning, the marten was gone, and Mistikôs had left a gift: a perfect marten pelt, soft as clouds.

Okimaw wore the pelt for the rest of his life. And when he died, the villagers found a marten sitting on his grave, its eyes bright, its fur wet with snow.

The Cree say: love is not possession. Love is letting go, and being surprised when the one you love comes back.
moral: You cannot keep what was never yours to keep. Love lets go, and is surprised when it is returned.
source: Based on Cree animal-marriage traditions from northern Canada.
